passage: Come, sit, Minakshi, and I'll tell you about the worst night of my first job, and why I'm so strict about rest now. I'm Afreen, and I was incident commander for a banking outage. By hour six the engineers were snapping at each other, and I saw one of them type the same command twice. I thought: tired minds make mistakes, and mine is one of them. So I stopped, called a break, and sent home the two who had been up since midnight to sleep. Fresh people took over, and I handed my notes to a colleague and rested for three hours myself. Some said I was wasting time. When I came back, the new team had found the fault in twenty minutes. Since then I plan handovers before an incident starts.

qa.q: What had one engineer done by hour six?
qa.a: One engineer had typed the same command twice.

qa.q: What was Afreen thinking when seeing the repeated command?
qa.a: Afreen was worried that tiredness was causing mistakes, including Afreen's own, which is why Afreen stopped everything.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Calling a break and bringing in fresh people made the difference, since tired engineers were making mistakes and the new team found the fault in twenty minutes.

qa.q: How might the two engineers sent home have felt at first?
qa.a: They may have felt reluctant to leave in the middle of the crisis, but they were probably also relieved, having been up since midnight.

grounding: Shows a commander who, knowing tired minds make errors, rotates people and sends the first responders to sleep before returning.

passage:
The data centre flood alarm went off at 10 p.m., and by 2 a.m. it was clear the recovery would run into the next day. Chetan, the incident commander, had a team of six on a video call, rain hammering on everyone's windows, two of them on generator power.
Jaya had been on it since the first alert. At 2.10 she typed, 'I'm fine, I'll keep going.' Chetan looked at her tired face and her typo-filled messages. 'No. Tired people make the worst mistakes in long incidents. Jaya and Sumit, hand your notes to Kiran and Pooja by 2.30 and sleep till nine. That's not optional.'
He wrote a rota in the channel: four-hour shifts, written handovers, commander changes at six. At 9.15 Jaya logged back in, rested, and within five minutes spotted a wrong setting the night shift had missed.

qa.q: By what time did Chetan ask Jaya and Sumit to hand over their notes?
What might Jaya have been feeling when she typed 'I'm fine'?
qa.a: Jaya was probably exhausted but reluctant to stop, feeling responsible and not wanting to look weak.

qa.q: What else could Chetan add to make handovers safer?
qa.a: He could use a short handover template, covering what's done, what's being tried and what not to touch, so nothing is lost between shifts.

qa.q: How did the rota help the team as a whole?
qa.a: Fresh people took over at night, and a rested Jaya caught a mistake in the morning, so the recovery was safer.

grounding: It shows a commander in a long incident rotating people every few hours and making sure the first responders sleep before returning.

passage:
By Saturday evening the outage at the Koramangala office had gone on for eleven hours. Avni, the incident commander, walked round the room. Chetan, who had taken the first alert at seven in the morning, was still at his desk, reading the same log line for the third time.
Avni stopped. 'Chetan, when did you last eat?'
'Lunch? I think.'
She thought it through aloud for the room. 'Long incidents are when tired people make the mistakes that start new ones. So: everyone who started before ten a.m. hands over by eight tonight. Write down what you've tried, what's running, what not to touch. Then go home and sleep. Back at eight tomorrow.'
Chetan opened his mouth to argue. Avni held up the handover template. He filled it in, slowly, and went home.

qa.q: When had Chetan taken the first alert?
What does Chetan reading the same log line three times suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was exhausted and foggy, too tired to take in information, even if he didn't feel ready to stop.

qa.q: Why did Avni ask for what not to touch in the handover?
qa.a: So the fresh shift doesn't undo work in progress or repeat risky steps, keeping the system state clear.

qa.q: How might the fresh team arriving at eight see the handover notes?
qa.a: They can start quickly with a clear picture instead of guessing what the tired team had already tried.

grounding: It shows a commander realising tired minds make errors in long incidents, rotating people and making sure first responders sleep before returning.
